data.title: How a Small Potash Developer Jumped A Massive Hurdle in Saskatchewan
data.description:
Key points

  • Buffalo Potash has connected all three horizontal wells underground at its Disley Project in Saskatchewan, proving its patented extraction design works in practice.

  • By showing fluid can reliably move between wells, Buffalo has cleared the prime technical risk that kept it trading at a discount to conventional potash miners.

  • The next step is pumping potash-rich brine to the surface ahead of a targeted Q1 2027 production start, though the project is still advancing without a formal feasibility study.

If you look at the world’s major potash mines, almost all of them belong to the major players like Mosaic (NYSE:MOS) or K+S. That’s not coincidental. Extracting potash traditionally requires sinking vertical wells and billions of dollars in infrastructure. 

That expenditure is typically a barrier to entry that’s kept smaller players on the sidelines. 

Buffalo Potash (TSXV:BUFF) is trying to rewrite the playbook on a prime patch of land in the middle of Saskatchewan. A plot that happens to border Mosaic’s Belle Plaine mine and K+S’ Bethune operation. Instead of drilling straight down with expensive vertical wells, Buffalo opted to lay three 565-meter horizontal wells along the base of the deposit. Essentially, one central injector flanked by two producers. 

Until this week, that exact setup was one of the reasons investors were staying cautious. Using horizontal wells to dissolve potash underground is the new kid on the block. 

Buffalo patented it and dubbed it the “Horizontal Line-Drive” (HLD) method, which has never proven its mettle at this scale. Mostly due to the fact that if the salty water pumped down doesn’t reliably reach the outer wells, the whole model is kaput. 

Question quelled

That question was just answered. Following its first well connection on November 23, Buffalo confirmed on the 25th that it’s connected the second producer well, completing an underground loop across all three wells. They’ve also reported pressure and fluid readings matching the subsurface engineering model predictions.

“Connecting the second producer well gives us confidence that what we're seeing underground is repeatable, which is exactly what we set out to demonstrate at this stage," CEO Steve Halabura said, noting the team is now laser-focused on delivering brine to the surface. 

For the investors 

So, what happens next (and why does it matter)? Simply put, Buffalo has cleared the engineering hurdle that often snags other runners. From here on, the process relies on the same solution-mining principles used across the region for 60 years which is to circulate brine, dissolve the potash and pump the mineral-rich liquid up for processing. 

Before it sees sunlight however, engineers will use an 11-stage packer system. Sounds complicated, but it’s essentially just a series of adjustable internal seals along the wells that pressurize different sections and widen the flow underground. 

This is also known as the Mining Plane.

Disley: by the numbers

Quick note: Economic figures come from Buffalo’s May 2026 Preliminary Economic Assessment. All the details can be found in Buffalo’s November 25 release.

What it all means

For investors, the broader story is the proof in the method’s pudding and how the tech can potentially shift Buffalo’s valuation narrative seeing as horizontal solution mining is designed to deliver lower operating costs and a smaller environmental footprint. 

Successfully proving it works at the Initial Production Module (IPM) gives Buffalo a repeatable, low-CapEx blueprint to build on. 

Once the company hits first production, still targeted for Q1 2027, the IP will be proven for deployment across other spaces at Disley, which can handily lead to scaling to a 1.125 million-metric-ton-per-year target.

What could still go wrong?

There is still plenty of executional risk between an underground connection and commercial cash flow. Buffalo is advancing the starter plant based on assessments rather than formal mineral feasibility reports. This means the real-world recoveries, costs and timelines can still vary wildly. They’re also working to finalize a royalty deal with Altius Royalty Corporation (announced October 22) to fund the remaining site and surface processing build-out. 

This article was written independently by the author, without issuer input or approval. Buffalo Potash has a marketing services agreement with Simply Wall St. Details on compensation and other important information can be found in the disclosure and disclaimer at the end of this narrative.

Technical and scientific information in this article is drawn from Buffalo Potash Corp’s news release dated November 25, 2026, which was reviewed and approved by independent Qualified Person Jared Galenzoski, P.Geo., FIMMM, in accordance with National Instrument 43-101. Readers should note that no mineral reserves have been established at the Disley Project, the company’s decision to advance the Initial Production Module is based on a Preliminary Economic Assessment rather than a feasibility study, and its Horizontal Line-Drive mining method has not yet been operated at commercial scale.

Main Street Capital has delivered a 5 year return that many income focused investors watch closely. The real question now is whether the current share price lines up with the returns the business actually earns on the capital it invests. With the stock recently closing at US$57.69, the issue is how much of those capital returns are already reflected in today's valuation.

  • Over the past 5 years the stock has gained 93.9%. This puts real weight on whether the returns Main Street Capital earns on its capital can support that kind of compounding over a full cycle.
  • Recent commentary around a potential US rate hike highlights that a higher base rate can increase interest income on Main Street Capital's partly floating rate loan book. This may support the level of returns it earns on each dollar deployed into its portfolio.
  • What if you looked at Main Street Capital through its earnings instead? See what Main Street Capital's 12.2x P/E says about the price.

For investors, the debate is whether the returns Main Street Capital earns on its capital are strong and durable enough to justify the price implied by that 5 year share performance.

If you want to test this same question about what return on capital really justifies today’s price across a wider income universe, scan through 39 dividend fortresses.

Is Main Street Capital Getting Expensive on Excess Returns?

The Excess Returns model looks at how much profit Main Street Capital can earn above its cost of equity on every dollar of book value. On this view the business is treated as a lender and investor, where long term value comes from earning more on equity than investors require over time.

For Main Street Capital, the inputs suggest a mature income engine rather than a high growth story. Book Value is $34.22 per share and Stable EPS is $3.56 per share, against a Cost of Equity of $3.04 per share. This leaves an estimated Excess Return of $0.53 per share, supported by an average Return on Equity of 11.13%. The model also anchors on a Stable Book Value of $32.03 per share and a long run dividend profile where analysts see growth capped at 3.91%, even though current dividends per share are $4.29. Recent focus on a possible December rate hike may help earnings on the floating rate loan book. Yet the Excess Returns projections still place intrinsic value substantially below the current US$57.69 share price. The Main Street Capital Narrative: What Would Justify Today's Price?

Narratives for Main Street Capital pick up where the valuation puzzle leaves off and spell out what would need to happen to growth, margins and earnings for the share price to look meaningfully higher or lower than it does today. Each narrative attaches a fair value to a clear storyline around Main Street Capital's potential drivers and threats, so you can track over time which version of events appears to be taking shape.

This Narrative is the analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St, which compiles analysts' consensus price target and revenue and earnings forecasts, not one person's view.

"The main thing that has to go right is that new lower middle market platforms and the expanded private loan and external management businesses keep producing realized gains and fee income…"

data.title: Have Insiders Sold Root Shares Recently?
data.description:
Anyone interested in Root, Inc. (NASDAQ:ROOT) should probably be aware that the Founder, Alexander Timm, recently divested US$198k worth of shares in the company, at an average price of US$40.21 each. However, the silver lining is that the sale only reduced their total holding by 3.4%, so we're hesitant to read anything much into it, on its own.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

Root Insider Transactions Over The Last Year

Notably, that recent sale by Alexander Timm is the biggest insider sale of Root shares that we've seen in the last year. So what is clear is that an insider saw fit to sell at around the current price of US$39.50. While insider selling is a negative, to us, it is more negative if the shares are sold at a lower price. In this case, the big sale took place at around the current price, so it's not too bad (but it's still not a positive).

You can see a visual depiction of insider transactions (by companies and individuals) over the last 12 months, below. If you click on the chart, you can see all the individual transactions, including the share price, individual, and the date!

View our latest analysis for Root

If you are like me, then you will not want to miss this free list of small cap stocks that are not only being bought by insiders but also have attractive valuations.

Insider Ownership Of Root

Looking at the total insider shareholdings in a company can help to inform your view of whether they are well aligned with common shareholders. A high insider ownership often makes company leadership more mindful of shareholder interests. It appears that Root insiders own 13% of the company, worth about US$77m. We've certainly seen higher levels of insider ownership elsewhere, but these holdings are enough to suggest alignment between insiders and the other shareholders.

So What Does This Data Suggest About Root Insiders?

An insider hasn't bought Root stock in the last three months, but there was some selling. And even if we look at the last year, we didn't see any purchases. On the plus side, Root makes money, and is growing profits. Insiders own shares, but we're still pretty cautious, given the history of sales. We're in no rush to buy! While it's good to be aware of what's going on with the insider's ownership and transactions, we make sure to also consider what risks are facing a stock before making any investment decision. Our analysis shows 2 warning signs for Root (1 can't be ignored!) and we strongly recommend you look at them before investing.

If you would prefer to check out another company -- one with potentially superior financials -- then do not miss this free list of interesting companies, that have HIGH return on equity and low debt.

For the purposes of this article, insiders are those individuals who report their transactions to the relevant regulatory body. We currently account for open market transactions and private dispositions of direct interests only, but not derivative transactions or indirect interests.
